questions.q: In the teleportation protocol, what resources do Alice and Bob need before Alice measures anything?
options: They need two separate, unentangled qubits with no prior relationship
Only Bob needs a qubit; Alice needs nothing but a classical description of |ψ⟩
Alice and Bob each independently prepare their own identical copy of |ψ⟩
Alice holds the unknown state |ψ⟩ plus her half of a pre-shared Bell pair, and Bob holds the other half of that same Bell pair
questions.explain: Teleportation requires a pre-shared entangled Bell pair split between Alice and Bob, plus Alice's original unknown qubit -- three qubits total, two of them entangled with each other.

questions.q: For |ψ⟩=0.6|0⟩+0.8|1⟩, if Alice's Bell measurement yields the Ψ+ outcome, what is Bob's qubit before correction, and what correction recovers |ψ⟩?
options: Bob's qubit is already (0.6, 0.8); no correction is needed
Bob's qubit is destroyed and cannot be recovered for this outcome
Bob's qubit is (0.6, -0.8); applying Z recovers (0.6, 0.8)
Bob's qubit is (0.8, 0.6); applying X recovers exactly (0.6, 0.8)
questions.explain: The verified teleportation table shows the Ψ+ outcome leaves Bob's qubit at (0.8, 0.6) -- the amplitudes swapped -- and applying X (which swaps amplitudes) recovers exactly (0.6, 0.8), the original state.

questions.q: Why does quantum teleportation NOT allow faster-than-light communication?
options: Bob cannot determine which correction to apply, and therefore cannot recover |ψ⟩, until he receives Alice's 2-bit measurement outcome over an ordinary classical channel, which cannot travel faster than light
Because the entangled qubits travel faster than light, compensating for the classical channel's speed limit
Because teleportation doesn't actually transmit any quantum information at all
Because Bob already knows the correct correction without needing any message from Alice
questions.explain: The protocol structurally requires Alice's classical 2-bit message to reach Bob before he can apply the right correction -- entanglement alone conveys no usable information, so nothing outruns the classical message's light-speed-limited travel time.

questions.q: Why is quantum teleportation consistent with the no-cloning theorem, rather than a violation of it?
options: Bob and Alice both end up holding a full copy of |ψ⟩ simultaneously after the protocol completes
Teleportation actually does violate no-cloning, which is why it only works probabilistically
No-cloning only applies to classical states, not quantum ones, so it's irrelevant to teleportation
Alice's original qubit is destroyed (collapsed) by her Bell measurement, so at every point in time exactly one copy of |ψ⟩ exists -- the state is moved, not duplicated
questions.explain: The key fact is that Alice's measurement destroys her copy of |ψ⟩ in the very act of transferring the information -- there is never a moment where two independent copies of |ψ⟩ coexist, which is exactly what no-cloning requires.

questions.q: What is the full resource cost of teleporting one qubit's state, according to the protocol worked through in this lesson?
options: Four separate entangled pairs, one for each possible measurement outcome
Nothing -- teleportation is entirely free once a quantum computer exists
Only the classical channel is needed; no entanglement is required at all
One pre-shared (and consumed) entangled pair, one Bell-basis measurement, and 2 classical bits of communication
questions.explain: The protocol consumes exactly one shared Bell pair (it cannot be reused), requires one joint Bell measurement by Alice, and needs exactly 2 classical bits sent to Bob so he can select the correct correction.
